opening.headline: Read Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework and distinguish what is similar and different from OpenAI and Anthropic's frameworks.
body: OpenAI calls it the Preparedness Framework, Anthropic calls it the Responsible Scaling Policy, and Google DeepMind calls it the Frontier Safety Framework. Although the three documents have different names and terminology, they are all promises to address the serious risks that even the most powerful models can pose.

In this lesson, you'll first read what Google's framework consists of and what the Core Competency Levels (CCLs) are. Next, we compare the terms, risk areas, and decision methods of the three companies in a table, and explain why the areas overlap but the terminology is different, and what criteria should be used when changing suppliers.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain risk areas and thresholds of the Frontier Safety Framework
You can distinguish the similarities and differences between the three company frameworks.

screens.title: What makes Google's safety framework different?
screens.lead:
Read about the challenges that arise for organizations when documents from three companies use different names and terminology.

As of 2026-10, RSP v3.4 is a policy that reads together Risk Mitigation Measures, Frontier Safety Roadmap, and Risk Reports. Descriptions of past ASL stages do not determine all current training and deployment conditions.

visual.alt: A scene of three document icons side by side, labeled with different terms, with a question mark in the middle.

paragraphs: An organization has been using one company's model and is considering moving to another company's model. My previous company's documentation had the level High and my new company's documentation had the word CCL. Security teams want to know whether the two terms mean the same level.

The three companies' documents have different names and terminology. However, this does not mean that they are unrelated documents. All promise to address the serious risks of the strongest models, measure capabilities, put in place safeguards, and put in place decision-making structures.
If you don't know the terminology, your standards will be shaken. This class covers reading Google's Frontier Safety Framework and then comparing the three companies side by side.

screens.outro: First, let's think about our experiences so far.

screens.title: Have you ever compared the frameworks of three companies?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't enter or submit your answer, so think for yourself first and then click.

items.prompt: Have you ever compared the frameworks of three companies side by side?
items.answer: When choosing a supplier, we often compare model performance and price, but rarely also compare safety frameworks. However, since these documents publicly promise how each company will manage risk, comparing them provides one more basis for choosing a supplier.

items.prompt: Have you ever heard of the term ‘core competency level’?
items.answer: Google's framework is built around thresholds called Critical Capability Levels (CCLs). If this is your first time hearing the term, you need to understand the role before the name. This is the threshold for the model's ability, at which point the risk becomes serious.

items.prompt: If I change the supplier, will the safety standards also change?
items.answer: As model providers change, the applicable safety framework also changes. Therefore, if the safety judgment standards used by an organization are tied to a specific company's terminology, they must be reorganized every time the supplier is changed. Setting standards based on areas and measures will reduce this burden.

screens.outro: First, let's take a step-by-step look at Google's framework structure.

screens.title: Basic structure of the Frontier Safety Framework
screens.lead: Select the arrow to the right to cycle through the four steps the Frontier Safety Framework addresses risk. It's helpful to see how each step builds on the previous step.

steps.title: Framework Purpose
steps.body: The Frontier Safety Framework (FSF) is a collection of protocols designed by Google DeepMind to safely and reliably develop its most powerful models: frontier models. The goal is to ensure that the model is reliable, well-tested, and consistent with human values.

steps.title: Step 1: Identify your competency level
steps.body: The frontier model determines at what level of capability the risk increases. This reference point is the Core Competency Level (CCL). You must first decide what to consider as a risk in order to measure and respond later.

steps.title: Step 2: Detect arrival
steps.body: We have protocols in place to detect whether that level of competency has been reached throughout the model's life cycle. Based on key early warning assessments, we perform a holistic assessment that includes systematic risk identification, comprehensive analysis of model capabilities, and explicit judgment of risk acceptability.

steps.title: Step 3: Prepare a mitigation plan in advance
steps.body: Proactively develop plans to reduce significant risks when competency levels are reached. Because it will be too late to make plans after you reach it. Once CCL is reached under this plan, a safety case review will be conducted prior to external release.

steps.title: Step 4: Involve external parties if necessary
steps.body: Where necessary or appropriate, engage external parties to inform and lead the approach. It is a device that checks from an external perspective whether internal judgment alone is sufficient.

steps.title: Documents and advancements used together
steps.body: FSF works in conjunction with Google's AI Principles and continues to evolve as new risks are identified. Because this framework addresses serious risks, its more general AI stewardship and safety activities are complemented by Google's other practices.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified the structure, let's read through the core competency levels and recent updates, focusing on terminology.

screens.title: Critical Capability Levels (CCLs) and Mitigation Measures
screens.lead: Hover over or select an underlined term in the description below to see a short description. Check the terms one by one.

data.text: FSF is centered around the threshold Core Competency Level (CCL). CCL represents the level of capability of frontier models to pose a significant risk of harm in the absence of mitigation measures. The updated version introduces CCL for harmful operations and expands the scope of Misalignment risk to include scenarios where models interfere with operators' instructions, modifications, or shutdowns of model operations. Machine learning R&D CCL addresses models that could accelerate AI R&D to unstable levels. Upon reaching such CCL, external release requires Safety Case Review, and large-scale internal deployments are also reviewed under R&D CCL. A later version introduced Tracking Capability Level (TCL) in certain areas to detect less extreme risks earlier.

terms.tip: Abbreviation for Critical Capability Level. The model is a baseline for the level of capability that, without mitigation measures, could increase the risk of serious harm.
It is a threshold aimed at the risk that models with powerful manipulation capabilities will systematically change people's beliefs and behavior in critical situations during interaction.
This is the risk that the model moves differently than the person intended. This extends to scenarios where the model interferes with operator instructions, modifications, and interruptions.
This is a safety case review. Detailed analysis is carried out prior to external release showing that risks have been reduced to a manageable level.
Tracked Capability Level. A new capability level introduced in some areas to enable early detection and assessment of less extreme risks than CCL.

data.notes: The risk areas in the table are representative of what each document publicly describes and are not exhaustive. The overlap in the same areas is because the three companies are assuming similar types of severe damage scenarios. On the other hand, terminology and decision methods are designed to fit each company's governance and organizational structure.

screens.outro: I will explain later why the difference in the table occurs.

screens.title: Explanation: Why areas overlap and terminology is different
screens.lead: Switch between the two views to see why the three frameworks are similar and different. It is a good idea to read this while thinking about what criteria to use when switching suppliers.

states.label: Why do areas overlap?
states.body: This is because all three companies assume similar types of extreme damage scenarios. Access to dangerous knowledge such as biology and chemistry, cyber attack capabilities, situations where AI accelerates AI research, and situations where models are beyond human control appear repeatedly. Since the types of risks are similar, the areas overlap, and the structures for measuring, installing safety devices, and making decisions are also similar.

states.label: Why are the terms different?
states.body: This is because each company designed its policies in accordance with its own governance, evaluation method, and organizational structure. One company centers a safety advisory group and management decision structure, another centers safety level steps and periodic reports, and another centers safety case reviews. Therefore, we cannot simply substitute that High and CCL are equal, and the definitions must be compared directly. When changing suppliers, organizations respond based on territory, actions, and decision-making methods, not terms. Specifically, it is practical to have three columns in our organization's rubric: risk area, required action, and decision-making entity, and fill in the columns by reading each company's document. Blank fields are a sign that the company's documents did not disclose the information, so this is a list of questions to ask directly to the supplier.

screens.outro: I will organize the comparisons from the perspective of the organization using them.

screens.title: The three frameworks address similar risks in different languages
screens.lead: Let's group the contents of this class into one standard. Read the paragraph below and move on to the final summary.

paragraphs: Our Frontier Safety Framework consists of four steps: identifying capability levels, detecting reach during the life cycle, preparing mitigation plans in advance, and involving external parties when necessary. Once the core competency level is reached, a safety case review is conducted prior to external release.

The three companies' frameworks address similar risks in different languages. Therefore, terms should be compared by definition rather than simple substitution. The basis for comparison is not the terminology, but the risk areas covered, the actions required, and the manner in which decisions are made.

For the user organization, this comparison serves as a basis for choosing a supplier. Rather than tying safety judgment criteria to one company's terminology, create your own table of criteria centered on areas and actions and map each supplier's documents to that table.

Also remember that the framework is an updated document. Our framework has also gone through several versions, adding new risk areas and new capability levels. Therefore, it is a good idea to write down the version of the document and the date it was verified in the rubric, and check for differences each time you reexamine the supplier.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: The framework is the provider's promise, and the purpose of the comparison is not to determine which company is better, but to find gaps in light of our standards.

glossary.def: A collection of protocols that Google DeepMind has put in place to safely develop the most powerful frontier models.
This is the threshold at which the model has the ability to increase the risk of serious harm in the absence of mitigation measures.
These are plans and safeguards put in place in advance to reduce risk when the CCL is reached.
A detailed analysis showing that the risk has been reduced to a manageable level. Upon reaching CCL, review prior to external release.
How to read the risk areas, terminology, and decision methods of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google side by side with the same criteria.

misconceptions.myth: The terms of the three companies are the same.
misconceptions.fact: Although the risk areas overlap, the terms are defined and the way they are determined are different. Words that seem similar, such as High and CCL, require direct comparison of definitions.

misconceptions.myth: The framework is a promotional document.
misconceptions.fact: A framework is an operational document that sets out a commitment to how evaluation, safeguards, and governance will operate. The reaching conditions and required actions are specifically written so that the using organization can read them as evidence.

misconceptions.myth: Knowing the standards of one company is enough.
misconceptions.fact: As the supplier changes, the framework applied also changes. By establishing your own standards centered on areas and actions, you can read any company's documents using the same framework.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: The three frameworks address similar risks in different languages.
The FSF consists of four phases: capability identification, detection, mitigation planning, and external engagement.
Once the CCL is reached, a safety case review occurs prior to external release.
Terms are compared by definition rather than simple substitution.
